claims.source: The zebrafish ear starts to sense body acceleration for the nervous system between 60 and 72 hpf, as demonstrated by the onset of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (Mo et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The ES begins to exhibit a physical behavior during the same time window (60-72 hpf).
claims.source: We found that the ES begins to exhibit a physical behavior during the same time window.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the live imaging data presented in Figures 1D-G.

claims.claim: The lumen of the ES remains closed until 60 hpf, but between 60 and 65 hpf it begins cycles of slowly inflating and rapidly deflating.
claims.source: We observed that the lumen of the ES remains closed until 60 hpf, but between 60 and 65 hpf it begins cycles of slowly inflating and rapidly deflating (sagittal slices, Figure 1D, lumen volumes, Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Videos 2–3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figures 1D-E and Videos 2-3.

claims.claim: The ES lumen volume changes 5–20-fold through the course of each cycle.
claims.source: Three-dimensional (3D) measurements showed that the ES lumen volume changes 5–20-fold through the course of each cycle (Figure 1E,F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figures 1E-F.

claims.claim: The period between peak ES volumes exhibited a broad distribution (0.3–4.5 hr) with an average of 1.6 ± 0.8 hr.
claims.source: The period between peak ES volumes exhibited a broad distribution (0.3–4.5 hr) with an average of 1.6 ± 0.8 hr (mean ± SD, histogram compiled from eight time courses and 54 peaks, Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of multiple time courses shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The duct is open and endolymph flows from the otic vesicle into the ES during inflation.
claims.source: We found that the duct is open and that endolymph flows from the otic vesicle into the ES during inflation (Figure 2A–D, Video 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dye injection experiments shown in Figure 2A-D and Video 4.

claims.claim: Upon deflation, endolymph rapidly leaked out of the ES and into the perilymphatic space.
claims.source: Additionally, upon deflation, endolymph rapidly leaked out of the ES and into the perilymphatic space (75:22 panel, Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Laser ablation of 2–3 cells within the wall of the otic vesicle distant from the ES at 64 hpf causes the ES to deflate and completely collapse within 20 min.
claims.source: To determine whether pressure in the otic vesicle is transmitted to the ES for its inflation, we laser-ablated 2–3 cells within the wall of the otic vesicle distant from the ES at 64 hpf (Figure 2E). Shortly after ablation, the ES deflated and completely collapsed within 20 min (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by laser ablation experiments shown in Figures 2E-F.

claims.claim: Fluid pressure in the otic vesicle inflates the ES volume.
claims.source: These results indicate that fluid pressure in the otic vesicle inflates the ES volume, the ES tissue has elastic material properties, and a loss of epithelial integrity is sufficient for ES deflation.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the laser ablation experiments shown in Figures 2E-F.

claims.claim: The ES tissue has elastic material properties.
claims.source: These results indicate that fluid pressure in the otic vesicle inflates the ES volume, the ES tissue has elastic material properties, and a loss of epithelial integrity is sufficient for ES deflation.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the rapid collapse of the ES after laser ablation shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: A loss of epithelial integrity is sufficient for ES deflation.
claims.source: These results indicate that fluid pressure in the otic vesicle inflates the ES volume, the ES tissue has elastic material properties, and a loss of epithelial integrity is sufficient for ES deflation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the laser ablation experiments shown in Figures 2E-F.

claims.claim: Perilymph dye begins to leak into the ES lumen at the onset of each deflation.
claims.source: Quantification of fluorescence within the lumen of the ES revealed that perilymph dye begins to leak into the ES lumen at the onset of each deflation (Figure 1F, visible leakage in Figure 1D, Videos 2–3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1F and imaging data in Figure 1D and Videos 2-3.

claims.claim: Deflation coincided with an influx of fluorescence from the perilymph into the lumen of the ES in each of the nine major inflation-deflation cycles.
claims.source: In the example shown deflation coincided with an influx of fluorescence from the perilymph into the lumen of the ES in each of the nine major inflation-deflation cycles.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Both deflation and dye leakage were due to transient breaks in the epithelial barrier.
claims.source: This coincident timing suggests that both deflation and dye leakage were due to transient breaks in the epithelial barrier, an interpretation that is consistent with the rapid release of endolymph prior to deflation (Figure 2D, Video 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the coincident timing of deflation and dye leakage shown in Figures 1F and 2D.

claims.claim: Endolymph efflux occurs at the same time as perilymph influx during deflation.
claims.source: To determine whether endolymph efflux occurs at the same time as perilymph influx, we simultaneously labeled the two fluids with different colored dyes and imaged their localization with higher temporal resolution (Figure 2G, Video 5). We found a fluttering behavior underlying deflation in which endolymph leaked out (62:41:20), perilymph leaked in (62:55:20), leaked-in perilymph flushed out with more endolymph efflux (62:55:40), followed by complete deflation (63:12:00).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dual-dye labeling experiments shown in Figure 2G and Video 5.

claims.claim: A plausible mechanism for the observed behavior involves a structure that normally resists flow driven by a pressure differential that rapidly opens during deflation to allow for fast efflux by advection followed by influx by diffusion before re-closing.
claims.source: A plausible mechanism for this observed behavior involves a structure that normally resists flow driven by a pressure differential that rapidly opens during deflation to allow for fast efflux by advection followed by influx by diffusion before re-closing.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed fluttering behavior during deflation.

claims.claim: The ES in lmx1bb mutants became greatly enlarged (>4 times the inflated wild-type ES volume) making it readily visible at 80 hpf by bright-field microscopy.
claims.source: We found that the ES in lmx1bb mutants became greatly enlarged (>4 times the inflated wild-type ES volume) making it readily visible at 80 hpf by bright-field microscopy (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The lmx1bb reporter (Tg(lmx1bb:eGFP)mw10) was expressed in ES cells beginning at 52–58 hpf, just before the first ES inflation.
claims.source: This reporter was expressed in ES cells beginning at 52–58 hpf, just before the first ES inflation (cyan, Figure 3B), consistent with lmx1bb expression being instrumental for development of the ability of the ES to release pressure.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging of the lmx1bb reporter shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The lmx1bb reporter expression is consistent with lmx1bb expression being instrumental for development of the ability of the ES to release pressure.
claims.source: This reporter was expressed in ES cells beginning at 52–58 hpf, just before the first ES inflation (cyan, Figure 3B), consistent with lmx1bb expression being instrumental for development of the ability of the ES to release pressure.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of lmx1bb reporter expression relative to ES inflation cycles.

claims.claim: Earlier in the development of the otic vesicle, lmx1bb is expressed in portions of the nascent semicircular canals and sensory patches, regions of the inner ear that also exhibit abnormal development in the mutant.
claims.source: Earlier in the development of the otic vesicle, lmx1bb is expressed in portions of the nascent semicircular canals and sensory patches, regions of the inner ear that also exhibit abnormal development in the mutant (Obholzer et al., 2012; Schibler and Malicki, 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on lmx1bb expression and mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: There is no precedent for ES development being dependent on those portions of the otic vesicles and there are many mutants with similar SCC or sensory defects that do not have ES phenotypes.
claims.source: There is no precedent for ES development being dependent on those portions of the otic vesicles and there are many mutants with similar SCC or sensory defects that do not have ES phenotypes (Fekete, 1999; Malicki et al., 1996; Whitfield et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on inner ear mutants.

claims.claim: The ES lumen over-inflates in lmx1bbjj410/jj410 mutant embryos.
claims.source: Live imaging and perilymph tracking in lmx1bbjj410/jj410 mutant embryos revealed that the ES lumen over-inflates (Figure 3C–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Videos 6–7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figures 3C-D and Videos 6-7.

claims.claim: In the lmx1bb mutant, perilymph was never observed entering the ES.
claims.source: In the mutant, however, we never observed perilymph entering the ES.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the quantification shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Endolymph leakage out of the distended ES epithelium was not observed in mutants where the endolymph was labeled.
claims.source: Additionally, we imaged mutants where the endolymph was labeled and did not observe leakage out of the distended ES epithelium (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The epithelial diffusion barrier remains intact in the mutant ES.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the epithelial diffusion barrier remains intact in the mutant ES.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the absence of perilymph entry and endolymph leakage in the mutant ES.

claims.claim: The ES tissue was much thinner in wild-type embryos during peak inflation than in the corresponding region in mutants inflated to a similar volume.
claims.source: Indeed, by comparing the dorsal ES tissue between wild-type and lmx1bb mutants using confocal microscopy and membrane-localized fluorescent proteins, we observed that the ES tissue was much thinner in wild-type embryos during peak inflation than in the corresponding region in mutants inflated to a similar volume (thin region indicated by asterisk, Figure 3F,G, data in G compiled from 65 to 80 hpf inflation events).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative analysis shown in Figures 3F-G.

claims.claim: In wild-type embryos, the thin region often appeared as a thin sheet (1.0 ± 0.3 µm, mean ±SD) rather than thick as seen in the un-inflated wild-type ES or the lmx1bb mutants in which two distinct surfaces (apical and basal) were observed (6.2 ± 3.2 µm).
claims.source: In wild-type embryos, this region often appeared as a thin sheet (1.0 ± 0.3 µm, mean ±SD) rather than thick as seen in the un-inflated wild-type ES or the lmx1bb mutants in which two distinct surfaces (apical and basal) were observed (6.2 ± 3.2 µm, the mutant, n = 9, is significantly thicker than wild-type, n = 14, with a Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon one tailed p-value of 4 × 10−5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The mutant ES is significantly thicker than wild-type (Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon one tailed p-value of 4 × 10−5).
claims.source: In wild-type embryos, this region often appeared as a thin sheet (1.0 ± 0.3 µm, mean ±SD) rather than thick as seen in the un-inflated wild-type ES or the lmx1bb mutants in which two distinct surfaces (apical and basal) were observed (6.2 ± 3.2 µm, the mutant, n = 9, is significantly thicker than wild-type, n = 14, with a Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon one tailed p-value of 4 × 10−5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of thickness measurements.

claims.claim: Imaging the uneven signal of the Tg(lmx1bb:eGFP) reporter revealed thin protrusions that extend along the basal side of neighboring ES cells.
claims.source: Imaging the uneven signal of the Tg(lmx1bb:eGFP) reporter revealed thin protrusions that extend along the basal side of neighboring ES cells (white arrow, Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: Sparse mosaic labeling of cells in the wild-type confirmed the presence of thin basal protrusions in the ES, as well as diversity in their organization.
claims.source: Sparse mosaic labeling of cells in the wild-type further confirmed the presence of thin basal protrusions in the ES, as well as diversity in their organization (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: Similar labeling in the mutant revealed the absence of thin basal protrusions in the ES.
claims.source: Similar labeling in the mutant revealed the absence of thin basal protrusions in the ES (Figure 3J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3J.

claims.claim: The basal surface of the ES tissue faces the perilymph outside surrounding the otic vesicle.
claims.source: We found that the basal surface of the ES tissue faces the perilymph outside surrounding the otic vesicle (Figure 3L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3L.

claims.claim: A clear difference in the staining pattern of collagen between wild-type and the lmx1bb410/410 mutant could not be resolved.
claims.source: We could not resolve a clear difference in the staining pattern of collagen between wild-type and the lmx1bb410/410 mutant.
claims.evidence: This is a negative result from immunostaining experiments.

claims.claim: Prior work suggested that Col1a2 may be a direct target of LMX1B in the limb.
claims.source: Prior work suggested that Col1a2 may be a direct target of LMX1B in the limb (Haro et al., 2017) and additional studies will be necessary to determine whether collagen or other extracellular matrix components are abnormally expressed in the ES of lmx1bb410/410 mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: ZO-1 stained the ES tissue that faces the endolymph-filled lumen.
claims.source: We also examined localization of the apical marker ZO-1 and found that it stained the ES tissue that faces the endolymph-filled lumen (Figure 3K–L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 3K-L.

claims.claim: This apical-basal organization was also present in the lmx1bb410/410 mutant.
claims.source: This apical-basal organization was also present in the lmx1bb410/410 mutant (Figure 3K–L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 3K-L.

claims.claim: The absence of local breaks in the mutant ES, the absence of regional thinning in the mutant inflated ES, and the absence of thin basal protrusions suggests that these thin areas may be structurally relevant to ES pressure relief.
claims.source: The absence of local breaks in the mutant ES, the absence of regional thinning in the mutant inflated ES, and the absence of thin basal protrusions suggests that these thin areas may be structurally relevant to ES pressure relief.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of wild-type and mutant ES structures.

claims.claim: The dorsal tissue of the inflated wild-type sac consists of an extremely thin shell of broadly overlapping lamellae extending from the basal sides of multiple adjacent cells.
claims.source: We found the dorsal tissue of the inflated wild-type sac consists of an extremely thin shell of broadly overlapping lamellae extending from the basal sides of multiple adjacent cells (Figure 4; Video 8).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figure 4 and Video 8.

claims.claim: These basal extensions appear to be the distal barrier in the ES because the endolymph they contain is continuous with the lumen of the ES and endolymphatic duct.
claims.source: These basal extensions appear to be the distal barrier in the ES because the endolymph they contain is continuous with the lumen of the ES and endolymphatic duct (extending ventrally from outlined ES lumen in third panel of Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the EM data showing continuity of the endolymph space.

claims.claim: Lamellar sheets extend for distances as long as a typical cell body but are as thin as 40 nm.
claims.source: We observed lamellar sheets that extend for distances as long as a typical cell body but are as thin as 40 nm (Figure 4A,F; lamella from cell segmented in purple extends 7.5 μm in the x-y plane and 6.6 μm along the z-axis).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from serial-section EM data shown in Figures 4A and 4F.

claims.claim: The lamellae from ES cells formed large zones of overlap and sometimes bifurcated to form a tongue-and-groove structure or interwoven structures.
claims.source: In contrast to junctions between thin aveolar cells, which kiss at their tips with tight junctions, the lamellae from ES cells formed large zones of overlap and sometimes bifurcated to form a tongue-and-groove structure (Figure 4B, inset) or interwoven structures (Figure 4C,F, black mesh highlights area of overlap, dotted perimeter indicates full spread).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figures 4B-C and 4F.

claims.claim: These structures lacked electron-dense signal, indicating that they were unlikely to contain tight junctions between lamellae.
claims.source: These structures lacked electron-dense signal, indicating that they were unlikely to contain tight junctions between lamellae.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of electron-dense signal in the EM data.

claims.claim: An ear was identified where the lamellar barriers were separated as if forced into an open configuration.
claims.source: We also identified an ear where the lamellar barriers were separated as if forced into an open configuration (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: This may be an ES in the act of deflating via bursting or sliding of the lamellae.
claims.source: This may be an ES in the act of deflating via bursting or sliding of the lamellae.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the EM data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The full serial-section EM dataset confirmed that the endolymphatic duct connects the lumen of the otic vesicle to the tip of the ES, where basal lamellae form a complete barrier.
claims.source: The full serial-section EM dataset also confirmed that the endolymphatic duct connects the lumen of the otic vesicle to the tip of the ES, where basal lamellae form a complete barrier (available at http://zebrafish.link/hildebrand16, ES-specific links presented in methods) (Hildebrand et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the full serial-section EM dataset referenced in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Basal lamellae were present along the length of the endolymphatic duct.
claims.source: Basal lamellae were present along the length of the endolymphatic duct.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the serial-section EM data.

claims.claim: Cell bodies in the duct remain tightly packed with apical junctions unlike the apical and lateral membrane separations exposing lamellae in the ES.
claims.source: However, cell bodies in the duct remain tightly packed with apical junctions (Figure 4A,E) unlike the apical and lateral membrane separations exposing lamellae in the ES.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figures 4A and 4E.

claims.claim: Electron-dense tight junctions are present in cells that also have spread basal protrusions.
claims.source: We identified electron-dense tight junctions between cells at the tip of the ES. These same cells also had lamellar projections (yellow arrows indicate tight junctions, Figures 4G and 3 serial EM sections, 1.2 μm apart, the diameter of the apical opening is ~1.2 μm).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The electron-dense signal formed a ring sealing the apical side of these ES cells that was continuous except for an opening that connected fluid from the duct and sac to the exposed lamellae.
claims.source: The electron-dense signal formed a ring sealing the apical side of these ES cells that was continuous except for an opening that connected fluid from the duct and sac to the exposed lamellae (magenta arrow directed from duct to sac, Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Apical junctions were also present in the mutant ES of lmx1bbjj410/jj410 larvae.
claims.source: Apical junctions were also present in the mutant ES of lmx1bbjj410/jj410 larvae (yellow arrows, Figure 4H,H').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figures 4H and 4H'.

claims.claim: The mutant ES appeared to completely lack openings in its apical junctions, as none were identified in mutants imaged by serial-section scanning EM or transmission EM.
claims.source: Unlike the wild-type ES, however, the mutant ES appeared to completely lack openings in its apical junctions, as we were unable to identify any in mutants imaged by serial-section scanning EM or transmission EM (four total mutant ears).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM and transmission EM data from mutant samples.

claims.claim: Long lamellar projections could not be found on the basal side of the mutant ES.
claims.source: Consistent with the absence of thin protrusions in the sparsely labeled mutants (Figure 3J), we could not find long lamellar projections on the basal side of the mutant ES (Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: Apical openings could not be identified in the wild-type ZO-1 immunostains.
claims.source: We were unable to identify apical openings in the wild-type ZO-1 immunostains (Figure 3L).
claims.evidence: This is a negative result from immunostaining experiments.

claims.claim: The inability to identify apical openings in ZO-1 stains could be due to difficulty resolving small openings (~1 μm diameter) or to ZO-1 remaining present at the openings such that the apical barrier could reform after ES deflation to hold hydrostatic pressure.
claims.source: This could be due to difficulty resolving small openings (~1 μm diameter) or to ZO-1 remaining present at the openings such that the apical barrier could reform after ES deflation to hold hydrostatic pressure.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about why apical openings were not observed in ZO-1 stains.

claims.claim: lmx1bb-dependent activity is necessary for openings to form in the apical junctions of ES tissue and for ES cells to extend thin basal protrusions.
claims.source: These data suggest that lmx1bb-dependent activity is necessary for openings to form in the apical junctions of ES tissue and for ES cells to extend thin basal protrusions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of wild-type and mutant ES structures.

claims.claim: The LLSM produced slightly blurred images with low signal-to-noise (SNR) without adaptive optics correction.
claims.source: The LLSM produced slightly blurred images with low signal-to-noise (SNR, Figure 5B) without adaptive optics correction.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Adding the correction with an AO-LLSM system adequately compensated for tissue aberrations and produced images with higher SNR and better contrast.
claims.source: Adding the correction with an AO-LLSM system adequately compensated for tissue aberrations and produced images with higher SNR and better contrast.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of images with and without AO shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Some cells stretched and thinned when the ES lumen was inflated and thickened upon deflation, likely a result of their elastic properties.
claims.source: We found that some cells stretched and thinned when the ES lumen was inflated and thickened upon deflation, likely a result of their elastic properties (Figure 5H,I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data and cell tracking shown in Figures 5H-I.

claims.claim: There were instances when the cells at the tip of the ES did not thin during inflation, or while they thinned during some events, they did not thin during others.
claims.source: However, there were instances when the cells at the tip of the ES did not thin during inflation, or while they thinned during some events, they did not thin during others (Figure 5J,K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data and cell tracking shown in Figures 5J-K.

claims.claim: For 43 of 99 tested trajectories, either cell thinning significantly correlated (p-value less than 10−3) with inflation or cell thickening significantly correlated with deflation.
claims.source: For 43 of 99 tested trajectories, either cell thinning significantly correlated (p-value less than 10−3) with inflation or cell thickening significantly correlated with deflation (green region, Figure 5L, example of significantly correlated interval, bracket with green arrowhead, Figure 5H, same data point indicated with green arrowhead in Figure 5L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of cell thickness trajectories shown in Figure 5L.

claims.claim: For 42 of 99 tested trajectories, cell behavior did not significantly correlate with inflation or deflation.
claims.source: For 42 of 99 tested trajectories, cell behavior did not significantly correlate with inflation or deflation (grey region, Figure 5L, example of uncorrelated inflation interval, bracket with grey arrowhead, Figure 5J, same data point indicated with grey arrowhead in Figure 5L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of cell thickness trajectories shown in Figure 5L.

claims.claim: For 14 of 99 tested trajectories there was significant correlation between inflation and cell thickening or deflation and cell thinning.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, for 14 of 99 tested trajectories there was significant correlation between inflation and cell thickening or deflation and cell thinning (magenta region, Figure 5L, example of correlated interval, bracket with magenta arrowhead, Figure 5J, same data point indicated with magenta arrowhead in Figure 5L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of cell thickness trajectories shown in Figure 5L.

claims.claim: Stretching of a subset of cells contributes to regulation of increased pressure by allowing the ES lumen to expand.
claims.source: While each cell's behavior is varied, these data suggest that stretching of a subset of cells contributes to regulation of increased pressure by allowing the ES lumen to expand.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cell tracking and correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Some cells appear to be pushed away from the ES lumen during inflation and pulled back into the ES epithelium during deflation.
claims.source: Additionally, some cells appear to be pushed away from the ES lumen during inflation and pulled back into the ES epithelium during deflation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cell tracking data showing unexpected correlations.

claims.claim: The complexity of the response is likely the result of features we did not resolve such as the dynamics of each cell's basal lamellae, each cell's residual apical and lateral adhesion, and each cell's basal interface with the extracellular matrix.
claims.source: The complexity of the response is likely the result of features we did not resolve such as the dynamics of each cell's basal lamellae, each cell's residual apical and lateral adhesion, and each cell's basal interface with the extracellular matrix.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the causes of the complex cell behaviors observed.

claims.claim: Some lamellae are rapidly extending and retracting like they are crawling over neighboring cells or neighboring lamellae.
claims.source: 3D rendering of the AO-LLSM signal shows that some lamellae are rapidly extending and retracting like they are crawling over neighboring cells or neighboring lamellae (Video 11).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data shown in Video 11.

claims.claim: Dynamic patches of increased intensity can shift rapidly in 3D renderings of the time course.
claims.source: In 3D renderings of the time course we see dynamic patches of increased intensity that can shift rapidly (Figure 6A, Video 11).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data shown in Figure 6A and Video 11.

claims.claim: Lamellae can crawl a few micrometers per minute.
claims.source: By merging 3D renderings of 3 consecutive time points, 30 s apart, in red, blue, and then green, we observed the relative displacement of these lamellae that can crawl a few micrometers per minute (Figure 6B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data and analysis shown in Figures 6B-C.

claims.claim: Inflations of the ES lumen coincided with slow increases in the surface area of exposed lamellae (30 min expansion).
claims.source: Inflations of the ES lumen coincided with slow increases in the surface area of exposed lamellae (30 min expansion, Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Some secondary loci included smaller lamellae that engaged and inflated much more quickly (1–2 min expansion).
claims.source: Some secondary loci included smaller lamellae that engaged and inflated much more quickly (1–2 min expansion, Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: The same locus can rapidly expand multiple times (one minute rapid expansions an hour apart).
claims.source: This presentation reveals that the same locus can rapidly expand multiple times (one minute rapid expansions an hour apart, Figure 6F,G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data shown in Figures 6F-G.

claims.claim: Multiple sets of basal lamellae can simultaneously engage at different loci, either through slow spreading or rapid expansion.
claims.source: In summary, multiple sets of basal lamellae can simultaneously engage at different loci, either through slow spreading or rapid expansion.
claims.evidence: This is a summary inference based on the AO-LLSM data showing different dynamics at different loci.

claims.claim: Myosin localized to the apical domains of ES cells as well as to dynamic puncta at the basal membrane throughout both inflation and deflation of the ES.
claims.source: Myosin localized to the apical domains of ES cells as well as to dynamic puncta at the basal membrane throughout both inflation and deflation of the ES.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging of myosin-GFP shown in Figure 6H and Video 12.

claims.claim: During ES inflation, contraction of apical myosin likely counteracts the stress of hydrostatic pressure and maintains the integrity of apical junctions.
claims.source: During ES inflation, contraction of apical myosin likely counteracts the stress of hydrostatic pressure and maintains the integrity of apical junctions (Rauzi et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed myosin localization and cited prior work on myosin function.

claims.claim: Tension from apical myosin, strain from hydrostatic pressure, and the adhesion strength between junctional protein complexes likely determines the elastic limit of apical junctions.
claims.source: Tension from apical myosin, strain from hydrostatic pressure, and the adhesion strength between junctional protein complexes likely determines the elastic limit of apical junctions.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanical factors determining apical junction behavior.

claims.claim: The crossing of this elastic limit may cause the small apical openings observed in Figure 4G, which ultimately communicates the otic vesicle's hydrostatic pressure to the lamellar protrusions.
claims.source: The crossing of this elastic limit may cause the small apical openings observed in Figure 4G, which ultimately communicates the otic vesicle's hydrostatic pressure to the lamellar protrusions.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of apical opening formation.

claims.claim: The dynamic spots of basal myosin could indicate two possible activities: contraction to retract lamellar protrusions as observed during cell migration or contraction at focal adhesions.
claims.source: The dynamic spots of basal myosin could indicate two possible activities: contraction to retract lamellar protrusions as observed during cell migration or contraction at focal adhesions.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the function of basal myosin puncta.

claims.claim: Utrophin localized strongest at apical domains of ES cells.
claims.source: Utrophin localized strongest at apical domains of ES cells (Figure 6H), but unfortunately bleached too quickly to generate any meaningful insights into the potential of actin localization dynamics.

results.result: The manuscript establishes foundational knowledge about inner ear anatomy and physiology, including the structure and composition of the endolymphatic sac (ES), the role of endolymph in hearing and balance, and the pathological consequences of pressure dysregulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C15-C16, and C18-C22 provide well-established anatomical and physiological context supported by citations and general knowledge. These foundational claims are necessary background for understanding the novel findings but do not constitute new discoveries themselves.

results.result: The ES undergoes cycles of slow pressure-driven inflation followed by rapid deflation, beginning between 60-65 hpf in zebrafish, with ES lumen volume changing 5-20-fold and cycling with an average period of 1.6 ± 0.8 hours.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C26-C32 are well-supported by live imaging data (Figures 1D-G, Videos 2-3) showing ES morphogenesis and quantitative measurements of inflation-deflation cycles. The temporal correlation with vestibulo-ocular reflex onset (C28) strengthens the functional significance. Sample size (n=8 time courses, 54 peaks) is adequate for the reported statistics.

results.result: Endolymph flows from the otic vesicle into the ES during inflation, and laser ablation of otic vesicle cells causes rapid ES deflation, demonstrating that otic vesicle pressure inflates the ES and that the ES tissue has elastic properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 are supported by dye injection experiments (Figure 2A-D, Video 4) and laser ablation experiments (Figure 2E-F). The ablation experiments (n=4) provide direct evidence that pressure transmission from the otic vesicle drives ES inflation and that loss of epithelial integrity causes deflation. The inference about elastic properties (C37) is reasonable given the rapid collapse after ablation.

results.result: Perilymph dye leaks into the ES lumen coincident with deflation, and dual-dye labeling reveals a fluttering behavior with simultaneous endolymph efflux and perilymph influx, suggesting transient breaks in the epithelial barrier.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 are supported by quantitative fluorescence measurements (Figure 1F) and dual-dye experiments (Figure 2G, Video 5). The coincident timing of deflation and dye leakage across 9 cycles provides strong evidence for transient barrier breaks. The proposed mechanism (C43) is a reasonable inference from the observed fluttering behavior, though it remains speculative about the specific structural basis.

results.result: In lmx1bb mutants, the ES becomes greatly enlarged (>4x wild-type volume) and over-inflates without deflation cycles, with no perilymph entry or endolymph leakage observed, suggesting the epithelial barrier remains intact but cannot release pressure.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C52 are supported by imaging data from lmx1bb mutants (Figures 3A-E, Videos 6-7). The lmx1bb reporter expression timing (C45, Figure 3B) correlates appropriately with ES inflation onset. The absence of perilymph entry and endolymph leakage in mutants (C50-C51) contrasts with wild-type and supports the inference that the barrier remains intact (C52). Sample sizes are adequate (n=4 mutant time courses).

results.result: Wild-type ES tissue during peak inflation is significantly thinner (1.0 ± 0.3 μm) than mutant ES tissue (6.2 ± 3.2 μm, p=4×10⁻⁵), with wild-type showing thin basal protrusions that are absent in mutants, suggesting these structures are relevant to pressure relief.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by confocal imaging and statistical analysis (Figures 3F-G) with appropriate sample sizes (n=14 wild-type, n=9 mutant) and a highly significant p-value. Claims C56-C58 documenting basal protrusions in wild-type but not mutants are supported by imaging data (Figures 3H-J). The inference about structural relevance (C64) is reasonable given the correlation between absence of these structures and loss of pressure relief function.

results.result: Serial-section EM reveals that the wild-type ES contains extremely thin (40 nm) overlapping basal lamellae forming lamellar barriers, with apical junctions containing small openings (~1.2 μm) connecting to the lamellae, while mutant ES lacks both the lamellar projections and apical openings.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C79 are supported by detailed serial-section EM data (Figure 4, Video 8) at 4.0×4.0×60 nm resolution. The ultrastructural characterization is thorough, including measurements of lamella thickness and extent (C67), documentation of overlap patterns (C68), and identification of apical openings (C75-C76). The mutant analysis (C77-C79) provides critical negative controls. However, the sample size is limited (n=2 wild-type, n=4 total mutant ears), which is acknowledged as a limitation due to the intensive nature of the technique.

results.result: AO-LLSM imaging reveals that some ES cells stretch and thin during inflation (43/99 trajectories significantly correlated), while others show no correlation (42/99) or unexpected inverse correlation (14/99), suggesting complex mechanical responses involving cell stretching and repositioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C89 are supported by AO-LLSM data with appropriate statistical analysis (Figures 5B-L). The correlation analysis of 99 cell trajectories using Spearman correlation (p<10⁻³ threshold) is methodologically sound. The heterogeneity in cell behavior (C85-C89) is well-documented. The inferences about mechanical contributions (C90-C91) are reasonable, though the speculation about unresolved features (C92) appropriately acknowledges limitations.

results.result: Basal lamellae are dynamic structures that crawl at speeds of a few micrometers per minute, with ES lumen inflations coinciding with slow increases in lamellar surface area (30 min) and some loci showing rapid expansion (1-2 min), with the same locus capable of multiple rapid expansions.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C99 are supported by high temporal resolution AO-LLSM data (Figures 6A-G, Video 11). The dynamic behavior of lamellae is well-documented through 3D renderings and temporal color-coding. The quantification of expansion rates and the observation of repeated expansions at the same locus provide strong evidence for the dynamic nature of these structures. Sample size (n=4 for AO-LLSM) is adequate given the intensive nature of the imaging.

results.result: Myosin localizes to apical domains and dynamic basal puncta throughout ES inflation and deflation cycles in both wild-type and lmx1bb crispants, suggesting consistent contractility that both resists pressure during inflation and drives deflation.
results.evaluation: Claims C100, C105, C108-C110 are supported by imaging data (Figure 6H-I, Video 12). The consistent apical localization throughout cycles (C100, C109) supports the inference about dual function (C108). However, the mechanistic interpretation (C101) relies partly on cited prior work and remains somewhat speculative. The utrophin data (C105-C107) provides limited additional insight due to bleaching issues, though the citation about utrophin not localizing to lamellae (C106) helps explain the observations.

results.result: The mutant ES rapidly collapses after otic vesicle puncture (5/5 experiments), and heat-shock induction of dominant negative Rac1 at 56 hpf (but not 32 hpf) causes ear leakage and collapse (19/34 vs 1/12 control), suggesting Rac1-dependent basal lamellipodia are important for barrier integrity during ES cycles.
results.evaluation: Claims C111, C114-C116 are supported by experimental data with adequate sample sizes (n=5 puncture experiments; 34 and 20 embryos for Rac1 experiments at different time points). The timing-dependent effect of Rac1 inhibition (C114-C115) provides strong evidence for the specific role of lamellipodia during ES cycling. The limitation acknowledged in C113 about interpreting global actin/myosin inhibition (C112) is appropriate.

results.result: AO-LLSM captures instances where membrane signal from lamellae is disrupted prior to deflation, and high temporal resolution imaging reveals narrow openings through which endolymph exits, observed in all high-resolution time-lapses (16 opening events in 4 fish).
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 are supported by AO-LLSM data (Figures 7A-E, Video 14). The observation of membrane disruption preceding deflation (C117-C118) and the identification of narrow release paths (C119-C120) provide direct visual evidence of valve opening. The consistency across multiple fish (4 fish, 16 events) strengthens the findings. This represents a key piece of evidence linking the structural observations to the functional deflation events.

results.result: The ES contains an lmx1bb-dependent pressure relief valve comprised of partially separated apical junctions and dynamic overlapping basal lamellae that separate under pressure to release fluid and maintain inner ear homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C82, C121, C140 represent the central conclusion synthesizing all experimental findings. The valve structure is supported by EM data (C6), the lmx1bb-dependence by mutant analysis (C82), and the function by the inflation-deflation cycles and their absence in mutants (C121, C140). While C7 extends the conclusion to "other fluid-filled cavities," this is supported by the comparative discussion of eye and kidney. The integration of structural and functional data across multiple techniques provides strong support for this major conclusion.

results.result: ES deflations may drive intermittent longitudinal flow of endolymph from the cochlea and semicircular canals, potentially explaining conflicting prior observations about tracer accumulation in the ES.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C126 are largely speculative (C122, C125, C126) about a secondary function of the ES. While C127 provides direct observation of flow during perilymph expulsion (Figure 2G, Video 5), this is a local phenomenon during deflation. The broader claim about longitudinal flow from other ear structures lacks direct evidence in this study. The citations to prior work (C123, C126) provide context but don't validate the proposed mechanism. This remains an interesting hypothesis requiring further testing.

results.result: LMX1 transcription factors may have conserved roles across ES, eye (Schlemm's canal), and kidney (podocytes) in apical junction remodeling to regulate fluid flow, as suggested by Nail Patella syndrome phenotypes and mouse models.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C139 draw connections between the ES findings and other organ systems. While the citations about Nail Patella syndrome and mouse models (C129, C132-C135, C137) are well-documented, the proposed common mechanism (C136, C139) is speculative. The structural similarity noted in C131 is interesting but insufficient to establish a common molecular mechanism. The inference about mouse Lmx1a and fish lmx1bb functional equivalence (C138) is reasonable but not directly tested. This represents an important hypothesis for future work but lacks direct experimental support in this study.

results.result: Several aspects of the valve mechanism remain unclear, including the molecular basis of lamellar organization, the role of extracellular matrix components, the determinants of the valve's set point, and how valve failure leads to disease symptoms.
results.evaluation: Claims C60, C80-C81, C102-C104, C143-C144, C147-C148 appropriately acknowledge limitations and identify important questions for future research. These include negative results (C60, C80), speculative mechanistic details (C102-C104, C144), and acknowledged gaps in understanding (C143, C148). This honest assessment of limitations strengthens the overall credibility of the work and provides clear directions for follow-up studies.
